articles.title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
articles.summary: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
articles.body: As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes. The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers. As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed. "Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated. Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity." "So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital. OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested. "For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients." Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic. "And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said. DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer. "The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result." Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer. "We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared. CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’ Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition. Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research. "If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower." "What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells." Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted. Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital. The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others. "For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said. Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said. "If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer. "More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Yendamuri emphasized the importance of continued funding for the National Cancer Institute, noting that it supports researchers working to advance cancer research and develop new discoveries.

articles.title: This Seasonal Habit Promotes Healthy Aging and May Reduce Dementia Risk in Older People
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, an oncologist reveals how routine vaccinations can promote healthy aging and protect against age-related decline.
articles.body: Aging is inevitable, but there’s increasing evidence that it may be possible to prevent, or at least delay, age-related diseases, including cardiovascular disease and Alzheimer’s. Although life expectancy has soared in the United States over the past century, many people are living longer in poorer health. That’s why many aging experts are shifting the focus away from lifespan. Instead, the goal is to maximize our “healthspan,” aka the number of years spent living into older age in good health. And slowing down biological aging often boils down to simple, healthy choices and preventive healthcare. Dr. Ezekiel Emanuel, an oncologist and professor of medical ethics at the University of Pennsylvania, previously spoke to TODAY.com about evidence-based habits to promote longevity, including staying up to date on routine vaccinations. There’s one vaccine in particular that’s especially important for adults over the age of 50, says Emanuel. Longevity Tip of The Day: Stay Up To Date With Your Flu Vaccine to Promote Healthy Aging If you’re an adult who wants to age healthier, get your annual flu shot, says Emanuel, who authored “Eat Your Ice Cream: Six Simple Rules for a Long and Healthy Life.” The seasonal influenza vaccine is the most effective way to protect against severe illness, complications and death from flu. In addition to these benefits, there’s growing evidence that the flu shot may protect against age-related neurodegenerative diseases. “Cognitive decline is a serious worry, so (getting the flu shot) is one thing you can and should do,” says Emanuel. Why It Matters As we get older, our body’s natural immune defenses gradually weaken, making it harder to fight off infections. People over the age of 65 face a much higher risk of getting very sick, becoming hospitalized or dying from the flu. “Thousands of people die every year from influenza,” says Emanuel. There’s increasing evidence showing that routine adult vaccines like the flu shot are associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer’s in older adults, TODAY.com previously reported. “Especially for people over 50, vaccines may reduce your risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” says Emanuel. In a 2026 study published in Neurology, researchers found that the high-dose flu shot is associated with a 55% lower risk of Alzheimer’s in adults over 65 in the years following vaccination. In addition to the flu shot, three other routine adult vaccines may cut dementia risk, says Ezekiel. These include the shingles vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, and the diptheria, pertussis tetanus vaccine (Tdap). So if you’re looking to protect your body and brain as you get older, staying up to date on these shots is crucial, Emanuel says. How to Get Started If you have questions about the flu shot or which vaccine is appropriate for you, talk to your doctor. The 2026-2027 seasonal influenza vaccines are available and being rolled out at pharmacies, doctors’ offices, hospitals and clinics nationwide. There are multiple options available, including egg-based standard dose flu shots, high-dose flu shots and cell-based shots. For the first time, there is also an mRNA flu shot available to those 50 and older this year (though the dementia reduction findings only apply to the other types of flu vaccines.) They protect against three flu viruses (two influenza A and one influenza B strain), which are expected to circulate this winter. The best time to get a flu vaccine is in late September or October, before flu activity peaks. It takes about two weeks for the flu shot to take full effect, and this protection generally lasts about six months through the end of flu season. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: NHS staff suspected of snooping on patient data to face immediate suspension
articles.summary: There have been too many cases of staff abusing patient trust, and enough is enough, the head of the NHS in England says.
articles.body:
NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping.

Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home.

NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches.

The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire .

This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death .

The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem.

The NHS said the "hardline" approach is part of a wider crackdown, including the launch of a national campaign to "remind staff of their responsibilities and the serious consequences of unlawful access".

"Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share," said NHS England's chief executive Sir Jim Mackey.

"We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough.

"Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record."

This month, an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years.

In some cases, it emerged staff were curious about a high-profile patient and wanted to know more about their condition or care.

Other staff have been struck off after looking up the medical records of relations, acquaintances and ex-partners without authorisation.

In 2023 an NHS consultant in Cambridgeshire was investigated by the General Medical Council (GMC) after accessing the health history of a woman who had started dating the doctor's ex-boyfriend.

There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access.

Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information.

IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when.

Paula McGowan, whose autistic son Oliver died in 2016 , was told that at least five members of staff at Southmead Hospital may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year.

Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete".

McGowan said she welcomed the NHS's commitment to tackling the problem but said it must now be followed by "meaningful action".

"Medical records contain deeply personal information about people and their families," she said.

"Accessing them without a legitimate clinical or professional reason is a serious breach of trust and must have consequences."

articles.title: A 100-Year-Old Woman Who Eats 1 Fruit Every Morning Shares 5 Simple Longevity Tips
articles.summary: A 100-year-old woman reveals foods she regularly eats, including blueberries, bacon and chocolate. She shares longevity tips such as dancing and knitting.
articles.body: When a 100-year-old shares her diet habits, it’s fascinating to consider which foods might be part of the longevity puzzle. For Natalie Groeger, bacon, blueberries and chocolate are regularly on the menu. She turns 101 in October and plans to celebrate with a party that will feature mushroom pizza, another favorite, and a drink. “Soda, not liquor,” she emphasizes in an interview with TODAY.com. The centenarian doesn’t drink alcohol. She was born in 1925 in a house in Brooklyn, New York; wed at 21 and worked as a switchboard operator, her favorite job. Groeger and her husband were married for 68 years, a union that produced two children, four grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. She now lives in an assisted living facility in Englewood, New Jersey. When asked what contributed to her longevity, she’s matter of fact. “I have no idea,” Groeger says. “You just have to be very open-minded, and you have to take it the way it is. That’s it. You have to take and enjoy living.” Here are some of her simple tips for a long life: Eat a Healthy Diet Groeger always starts her breakfast with blueberries. “I eat a lot of blueberries. I love them,” she says. Registered dietitian Samantha Cassetty picks blueberries as the healthiest fruit because of all the health benefits they provide. Blueberries have been linked to a lower risk of heart disease and Type 2 diabetes, and improvements in cognitive performance, she notes. Groeger has also been a life-long fan of apples, which have benefits for heart health, diabetes, cancer, gut health, weight loss and inflammation. She enjoys avocados, a creamy fruit that research links with heart health, skin health and weight management. The centenarian doesn’t have a specific diet she follows: “I eat basically everything,” she says. Enjoy a Treat Groeger loves chocolate, especially the dark kind, which is considered to be the healthiest chocolate. Dark chocolate contains the most cocoa bean solids, which have phytochemicals shown to have anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and antihypertensive properties, dietitians say. Another favorite treat would probably get less approval from nutrition experts. “I love bacon,” Groeger says. “I probably shouldn’t eat bacon, but I eat it.” Her breakfast regularly includes two over-easy fried eggs with bacon and an English muffin. Other centenarians have expressed love for bacon. But just because they can indulge and live a long life doesn’t mean everyone can. They have a very rare combination of protective genes that reduces their risk for age-related diseases, Dr. Thomas Perls, director of the New England Centenarian Study, previously told TODAY.com. Dance The centenarian loves ballroom dancing and taught her husband how to dance. Every Sunday after breakfast, she would put on records and the couple would dance “all over the living room and dining room,” she recalls. Groeger also recalls dancing at the Brooklyn Academy of Music when she was 20. “I felt like a Rockette because that’s how high my legs went up. But I can’t do it anymore,” she says. Today, she’s still moving to music by taking part in chair dancing. Dancing is both aerobic and weight-bearing exercise that comes with many benefits including better heart health, balance and coordination; plus improved mood and a lower risk of dementia, the National Library of Medicine notes. It’s also incredibly social and fun. Try a Hobby to Calm Your Mind Groeger’s mom taught her how to knit when she was a young girl and she’s been knitting much of her life, creating blankets, hats and sweaters. She stopped only a couple of years ago because of hand issues. Crafting comes with mental health benefits. For example, crochet makes people feel calmer and happier, with people using it to manage grief, chronic illness and pain, a study found. The centenarian also likes playing solitaire on her iPad and Canasta, a card game, with friends. Board and card games can help older people maintain cognitive functions, studies have found. Don’t Take Things Too Seriously Everyone experiences stress, but the ability to manage it can be a factor in longevity, researchers note. Groeger tries not to dwell on obstacles that come in life. “I’m the type of person who doesn’t talk really about my problems, and that makes life easier for me,” she says. “I’m a happy person. I like to laugh. I like to joke around. I used to be a very good storyteller and a dirty joke teller.” Being under heavy stress shortens life expectancy by almost three years — more than the lack of exercise, a study found. There’s a “significant relationship between cumulative stress and age acceleration,” but “psychological resilience,” emotion regulation and self-control can slow that process, researchers reported in a separate paper. Be an Optimist In a related trait, optimism is associated with “exceptional longevity,” or living to age 85 and beyond, studies have found. “I’m definitely an optimist,” Groeger says. “I think everything is going to be good. Even though I’ve had some bad times in my life.” People with higher levels of optimism tend to have healthier cardiovascular, metabolic, immune and pulmonary systems, leading to an 11-15% longer life span, the study authors note. Optimism may promote healthier behaviors and foster protective coping mechanisms such as “reframing situations as challenges rather than threats,” they add.
